title: Frozen Knowledge Can Be Deadly
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Using the (likely apocryphal) story of Einstein reusing the same Princeton final exam because "the answers keep changing," the piece argues that knowledge which stays static becomes frozen and dangerous for leaders. Leaders who sit in a role for a long time come to rely on facts and assumptions that have quietly gone out of date. The authors propose a deliberately pessimistic default: assume that whatever facts you depend on are outdated or wrong after a year or two. They name the core obstacle as leaders' resistance to relearning what they think they already know. The remedy is concrete: write down the key facts and assumptions you operate from and revisit them by reading and listening to subject-matter experts. The closing claim is that frozen knowledge can be more dangerous than no knowledge at all, so a leader's knowledge must keep evolving even when the questions stay the same.
points: The Einstein exam story frames the point: the questions a leader faces can stay constant while the right answers shift underneath them.
A practical rule of thumb: presume the facts you rely on are outdated or wrong after a year or two rather than assuming they still hold.
The hardest barrier is psychological, since leaders resist learning what they believe they already know.
Make assumptions explicit by writing them down, then test them against current expert reading and conversation.
Stale knowledge is framed as worse than ignorance because it carries false confidence into decisions.
quotes: Knowledge that stays static in any way becomes frozen in time. As leaders sit in a given role for a long period of time, frozen knowledge can create havoc with their decisions and choices.
The challenge for every leader is to test and retest the assumptions they make about the knowledge claims central to their work.

So, the safe bet is to presume whatever so-called facts a leader relies upon are generally outdated or just plain wrong after a year or two. Here’s the kicker. Leaders always resist learning what they think they already know.
Write down the key facts and assumptions you operate from and spend a little time reading and listening to subject-matter experts about them.
Frozen knowledge is sometimes more dangerous than no knowledge at all. Leaders and what they know must continue to evolve, even while the questions stay static.
